1.pericope_label: Now in the twenty and fourth day of this month the children of Israel were assembled with fasting, and with sackclothes, and earth upon them

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch date the assembly two days after the closing gathering of tabernacles and deny that the separation from strangers concerns heathen marriages at all — against Bertheau, it is neither that nor a rule of admission but "a voluntary renunciation of connection with the heathen, and of heathen customs." Ellicott marks only one day of rest before the fast, finds a deep propriety in the change of word to "seed", divides both day and night into four parts with reading in the morning and worship in the afternoon, and locates the seam between the two lists of Levites in the pronoun — "their God" at verse 4, "your God" at verse 5 — concluding that these eight offered a prayer which is not inserted.

Gill dates the fast two days after tabernacles ended, takes the separation of Israelites from Gentile wives as "a proof of the truth of their repentance", places the standing in the outward court where men prayed and confessed, and identifies the Levites' platform as the elevated place from which they sang at the time of sacrifice.

Clarke reconstructs the whole month day by day, putting the separation on the twenty-third and the fast on the twenty-fourth, follows Calmet in dividing the daylight into four stretches and the exercises into three, and turns the summons to stand into a rebuke of his own century's "shameless custom of many congregations of people to sit still while they profess to bless and praise God." Wesley supplies the motive — a grief the season of public joy had not allowed them to express — and takes the several pulpits to mean the congregation divided between the Levites.

Henry reads the day against Isaiah 58: a fast that men appointed but such a fast as God had chosen, both a day to afflict the soul and a day to loose the bands of wickedness, "without this, spreading sackcloth and ashes under us is but a jest." He widens the separation to the strange children as well as the strange wives, reports Bishop Patrick's twelve-hour reckoning beside his own six, and insists on the reciprocity of word and prayer — "fasting without prayer is a body without a soul, a worthless carcase."

debates.question: What did the separation from strangers in verse 2 consist of?

positions.view: The putting away of Gentile wives married before or since Ezra's reformation, proving the reality of their repentance
That and more — the strange children as well as the strange wives, since those who join themselves to God by covenant must separate themselves from sin and sinners
Not the marriages at all, nor a rule of admission to the assembly, but a voluntary renunciation of connection with the heathen and of heathen customs

debates.question: How long did the fourth parts of the day run?

positions.view: About three hours each, six hours in all
The whole twelve hours of daylight, in four equal stretches

debates.question: Why are the Levites named twice, in verses 4 and 5?

positions.view: Either they prayed successively, one by one, or there were eight congregations each with a Levite presiding
Two distinct acts by the same men: first crying to God themselves, then calling the congregation to worship
The pronoun shifts from "their God" to "your God", so the eight offered a prayer which the text does not record

outliers.claim: Reports that the Septuagint drops every name after Kadmiel and inserts "and Ezra said" before verse 6, and thinks the psalm may be Ezra's composition though uttered by the Levites for the congregation.

themes: Now in the twenty and fourth day of this month the children of Israel were assembled with fasting, and with sackclothes, and earth upon them.
And the seed of Israel separated themselves from all strangers, and stood and confessed their sins, and the iniquities of their fathers.
And they stood up in their place, and read in the book of the law of the Lord their God one fourth part of the day; and another fourth part they confessed, and worshipped the Lord their God.
Then stood up upon the stairs, of the Levites, Jeshua, and Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani, and cried with a loud voice unto the Lord their God.

Then the Levites, Jeshua, and Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabniah, Sherebiah, Hodijah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah, said, Stand up and bless the Lord your God for ever and ever: and blessed be thy glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise.

6.pericope_label: Thou, even thou, art LORD alone; thou hast made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their host

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch show the verse enlarging its terms deliberately — heaven by "heaven of heavens", earth by "the sea and all therein" — with "all their host" belonging only to the heaven clause. Ellicott takes the worshipping host for angels rather than stars, finds the comprehensiveness of the verse reproduced only at Hebrews 1:3, notes that the Hivites are omitted from the covenant grant, observes that five of the names given to the law in Psalm 119 are gathered at Sinai though the weight rests on the adjectives, and reads the sabbath clause forward to the covenant of the next chapter.

Gill locates the life in the divine nature, reads the choice of Abram as a calling out from among the Chaldeans and out of his father's family, takes the faithful heart as proved in the offering of Isaac, and insists that God was "not a mere spectator" of the affliction in Egypt but looked upon it with pity and sent a deliverer. The sabbath he treats as Israel's peculiar privilege, rest both corporeal and spiritual, typical of the rest in Christ.

Clarke renders the Hebrew strictly — "thou givest life to them all" — and entertains Kepler's notion that the heavenly host are instinct with life before withdrawing it, since to preserve in being does not necessarily imply vitality. He supposes the sabbath had been forgotten during the sojourn in Egypt and so had to be made known again. Wesley grounds the moral and judicial precepts in natural equity and reads the ceremonial ones as tokens of goodness and types of gospel grace.

Henry sets out the adoration in four articles — the only living and true God, the Creator, the Protector, and the object of the creatures' praises — and refuses to let "foundest his heart faithful" be a discovery: God found it so "because he made it so (for faith is not of ourselves, it is the gift of God)." He reads the pillar as settling the timetable and not the route only, and sums the wilderness provision as food convenient in the way with the good land at journey's end.

debates.question: Who is the host of heaven that worships?

positions.view: Possibly the stars themselves, if Kepler was right that they are instinct with life — though the verb need not imply vitality

debates.question: What does it mean that God "madest known" the sabbath?

positions.view: A privilege peculiar to Israel, typical of the rest in Christ
A restoration: they had forgotten this first of all the commandments during the sojourn in Egypt
A forward pointer, its prominence here marking its weight in the covenant of chapter 10 and throughout the book

outliers.claim: Measures every doxology against its object: "put all the praises of heaven and earth together, and the thousandth part is not said of what might and should be said of the glory of God."

themes: Thou, even thou, art Lord alone; thou hast made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their host, the earth, and all things that are therein, the seas, and all that is therein, and thou preservest them all; and the host of heaven worshippeth thee.
Thou art the Lord the God, who didst choose Abram, and broughtest him forth out of Ur of the Chaldees, and gavest him the name of Abraham;

And foundest his heart faithful before thee, and madest a covenant with him to give the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, and the Perizzites, and the Jebusites, and the Girgashites, to give it, I say, to his seed, and hast performed thy words; for thou art righteous:
And didst see the affliction of our fathers in Egypt, and heardest their cry by the Red sea;

And shewedst signs and wonders upon Pharaoh, and on all his servants, and on all the people of his land: for thou knewest that they dealt proudly against them. So didst thou get thee a name, as it is this day.
And thou didst divide the sea before them, so that they went through the midst of the sea on the dry land; and their persecutors thou threwest into the deeps, as a stone into the mighty waters.
Moreover thou leddest them in the day by a cloudy pillar; and in the night by a pillar of fire, to give them light in the way wherein they should go.
Thou camest down also upon mount Sinai, and spakest with them from heaven, and gavest them right judgments, and true laws, good statutes and commandments:
And madest known unto them thy holy sabbath, and commandedst them precepts, statutes, and laws, by the hand of Moses thy servant:

And gavest them bread from heaven for their hunger, and broughtest forth water for them out of the rock for their thirst, and promisedst them that they should go in to possess the land which thou hadst sworn to give them.

16.pericope_label: But they and our fathers dealt proudly, and hardened their necks, and hearkened not to thy commandments

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that "dealt proudly" is the very word used of the Egyptians six verses earlier, corrects "divide them into corners" to a division of the nations unto Israel within their boundaries, observes that the Spirit's teaching function occurs only here in the Old Testament and anticipates the New, and finds the phraseology of Judges carefully remembered in the prayer. Keil and Delitzsch supply the limit asserted at verse 31: God did not suffer his people to become extinct in exile but preserved a remnant.

Gill reads the rebellion as haughtiness towards a kind benefactor, traces the molten calf to the Apis of Egypt, reports the Jewish readings of the good Spirit as the spirit of prophecy or that put upon the seventy elders, and offers an alternative rendering of the forbearance — "thou didst draw upon them" — which Jarchi takes of mercy drawn out of God's own heart.

Clarke works by textual repair and historical parallel: bemiryam is a copyist's error for bemitsrayim, so the captain was appointed to return to bondage in Egypt; the conjunction at verse 22 should be read "even", since only one king of Heshbon can be meant; the cloud took three distinct postures; and the prosperity of verse 25 follows an old maxim he matches from Sallust. Wesley closes the gap between resolving and doing by intention, as Abraham is said to have offered Isaac because he intended to.

Henry makes pride the root rather than the symptom of disobedience and names two failures of attention behind it — hearing without hearkening, seeing without being mindful. He insists deliverance was never a verdict on the delivered, God giving them saviours "not for any merit of theirs", and testifying against their sins in the very act of rescue lest they misconstrue deliverance as connivance. From the prophets' testimony he draws a rule for ministry: bring people to God by bringing them to his law, "not to bring them to ourselves by bringing them under any law of ours."

debates.question: Did they appoint a captain "in their rebellion" or "to return to Egypt"?

positions.view: To Egypt — bemiryam is a scribal error for bemitsrayim, as several manuscripts, the Septuagint and Numbers 14:4 read
The difficulty is not textual but moral: at Numbers the return was only resolved on, and they are said to have done what they intended

outliers.claim: Sets an old English saying beside a sentence of Sallust to explain the collapse after the conquest: "war begets poverty, poverty begets peace, peace begets affluence, affluence begets luxury and corruption of manners; and hence civil broils, foreign wars, and desolations."
Holds the ruin to have been wholly gratuitous — Canaan could not have made them happier, "had it not been their own fault."

themes: But they and our fathers dealt proudly, and hardened their necks, and hearkened not to thy commandments,

And refused to obey, neither were mindful of thy wonders that thou didst among them; but hardened their necks, and in their rebellion appointed a captain to return to their bondage: but thou art a God ready to pardon, gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and forsookest them not.
Yea, when they had made them a molten calf, and said, This is thy God that brought thee up out of Egypt, and had wrought great provocations;

Yet thou in thy manifold mercies forsookest them not in the wilderness: the pillar of the cloud departed not from them by day, to lead them in the way; neither the pillar of fire by night, to shew them light, and the way wherein they should go.
Thou gavest also thy good spirit to instruct them, and withheldest not thy manna from their mouth, and gavest them water for their thirst.
Yea, forty years didst thou sustain them in the wilderness, so that they lacked nothing; their clothes waxed not old, and their feet swelled not.
Moreover thou gavest them kingdoms and nations, and didst divide them into corners: so they possessed the land of Sihon, and the land of the king of Heshbon, and the land of Og king of Bashan.
Their children also multipliedst thou as the stars of heaven, and broughtest them into the land, concerning which thou hadst promised to their fathers, that they should go in to possess it.

So the children went in and possessed the land, and thou subduedst before them the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, and gavest them into their hands, with their kings, and the people of the land, that they might do with them as they would.

And they took strong cities, and a fat land, and possessed houses full of all goods, wells digged, vineyards, and oliveyards, and fruit trees in abundance: so they did eat, and were filled, and became fat, and delighted themselves in thy great goodness.

Nevertheless they were disobedient, and rebelled against thee, and cast thy law behind their backs, and slew thy prophets which testified against them to turn them to thee, and they wrought great provocations.

Therefore thou deliveredst them into the hand of their enemies, who vexed them: and in the time of their trouble, when they cried unto thee, thou heardest them from heaven; and according to thy manifold mercies thou gavest them saviours, who saved them out of the hand of their enemies.

But after they had rest, they did evil again before thee: therefore leftest thou them in the hand of their enemies, so that they had the dominion over them: yet when they returned, and cried unto thee, thou heardest them from heaven; and many times didst thou deliver them according to thy mercies;

And testifiedst against them, that thou mightest bring them again unto thy law: yet they dealt proudly, and hearkened not unto thy commandments, but sinned against thy judgments, (which if a man do, he shall live in them;) and withdrew the shoulder, and hardened their neck, and would not hear.
Yet many years didst thou forbear them, and testifiedst against them by thy spirit in thy prophets: yet would they not give ear: therefore gavest thou them into the hand of the people of the lands.
Nevertheless for thy great mercies’ sake thou didst not utterly consume them, nor forsake them; for thou art a gracious and merciful God.

32.pericope_label: Now therefore, our God, the great, the mighty, and the terrible God, who keepest covenant and mercy

schools.summary: Ellicott marks verse 32 as the beginning of the prayer proper, identifies the kings of Assyria as the rod of God's anger, flags the omission of the prophets from the list of transgressors, and relocates the distress: it lies "not so much under the Persian yoke as in the remembrance of God's judgments", the passage turning almost word by word on the contrast between what the land was given for and what it has become. Keil and Delitzsch reduce the plea to a sentence, keep the received "in their kingdom" of the days of independence, and trace the description of the land to Exodus 3:8.

Gill hears Nehemiah's own titles for God in the opening words and concludes the whole prayer is his composition, delivered by him to the Levites; he grants the justice of the sentence without reserve, notes that leave to return did not end subjection to Persia, and reads the closing formula with Jarchi as "in all this distress" rather than "because of all this."

Clarke reads the roll of sufferers as a social ladder and the bondage as political oppression — tribute exacted at the sovereign's pleasure, "so that we can neither call our persons, our time, our land, nor our cattle, our own" — before turning on his own readers, and he takes the sealed covenant as evidence of a mixed aristocracy in which church and state were separate but mutually supporting. Wesley explains the joining of mercy to covenant, since the covenant alone "was not a sufficient ground of hope", and makes the confession of God's justice a rule for all sufferers.

Henry spreads the guilt across kings, princes, priests and fathers, "and we in them", and finds the sentence fitted to the offence: those who would not serve God in their own land were made to serve their enemies in a strange one, exactly as Deuteronomy had threatened.

debates.question: Should verse 35 read "in their kingdom" or "in thy kingdom"?

positions.view: "In thy kingdom" — the reading of Kennicott's manuscripts and of the Septuagint, Syriac and Arabic, and most likely the true one
"In their kingdom", that is, while the kingdom was still independent

debates.question: What is the great distress of verse 37?

positions.view: Political subjection: tribute and forced service exacted at the sovereign's pleasure, so that nothing can be called their own
Not the Persian yoke so much as the remembrance of God's judgments

outliers.claim: Ascribes the whole prayer to Nehemiah himself on the evidence of its divine titles, delivered by him to the Levites to utter — against the suggestion elsewhere in the chapter that Ezra composed it.

Reads the omission of the prophets from the list of transgressors as deliberate tribute: they alone "continued faithful to God, testifying by his Spirit against the crimes of all, even at the risk of their lives."

themes: Now therefore, our God, the great, the mighty, and the terrible God, who keepest covenant and mercy, let not all the trouble seem little before thee, that hath come upon us, on our kings, on our princes, and on our priests, and on our prophets, and on our fathers, and on all thy people, since the time of the kings of Assyria unto this day.
Howbeit thou art just in all that is brought upon us; for thou hast done right, but we have done wickedly:
Neither have our kings, our princes, our priests, nor our fathers, kept thy law, nor hearkened unto thy commandments and thy testimonies, wherewith thou didst testify against them.

For they have not served thee in their kingdom, and in thy great goodness that thou gavest them, and in the large and fat land which thou gavest before them, neither turned they from their wicked works.
Behold, we are servants this day, and for the land that thou gavest unto our fathers to eat the fruit thereof and the good thereof, behold, we are servants in it:

And it yieldeth much increase unto the kings whom thou hast set over us because of our sins: also they have dominion over our bodies, and over our cattle, at their pleasure, and we are in great distress.
And because of all this we make a sure covenant, and write it; and our princes, Levites, and priests, seal unto it.
